pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–9 years

- **Topic:** Earth's Layers — Earth has a thin outer crust, a thick hot mantle and a core at the centre, and the inside of the Earth is extremely hot (hot enough to melt rock).

- **Standards — UK (KS2, mixed placement):** England has NO KS2 science requirement on Earth's internal structure; 'the composition of the Earth' and 'the structure of the Earth' are DfE **KS3 Chemistry — Earth and atmosphere**. At KS2 this content lives in **Geography** (physical geography: volcanoes and earthquakes) and builds on Y3 **Rocks** ('Earth is made of rock'). Treat as an enrichment/Geography-linked topic that runs ahead of the KS2 science sequence.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** Earth's internal layers are not a standalone elementary PE; systems and materials of Earth appear across **4-ESS2** and the interior is formally treated at **MS-ESS2** (Earth's materials and systems / plate tectonics history). Nearest young-learner touchpoints: 2-ESS1-1 (Earth events) and 4-ESS2-2 (patterns of features). State-standard tier: DEFERRED.

- **Operational details:** Prerequisite is 'Earth Is Made of Rock' (5–7). Deliver three named layers (crust, mantle, core) on one cutaway, and land two comparative ideas that are the real payload: the crust is astonishingly THIN relative to the whole, and it gets HOTTER with depth (hot enough to melt rock). Use a scale analogy (apple skin / eggshell) for the thin crust.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, model + scale). The insights are proportional (thin crust) and comparative (hotter with depth) rather than mechanistic. Expect children to over-estimate crust thickness and to imagine a hollow or watery interior. Success = name the three layers, state the crust is thinnest, and state the interior is hot enough to melt rock.
bestPractices: Introduce all three layers on ONE labelled cutaway sphere, largest-to-smallest by name, before adding any facts — keep the model singular and stable.
Make 'thin crust' concrete with a whole-object scale analogy the child can hold in mind: the crust is like the skin on an apple or the shell of an egg compared with everything beneath.
Teach 'hotter with depth' as a felt gradient — not just 'the core is hot' but 'the deeper you go, the hotter, until rock itself melts' — linking to why magma exists (bridge to 'Inside a Volcano').
Distinguish solid crust and (mostly) solid mantle from the very hot core; avoid implying the whole inside is liquid lava.
Use drill-down/zoom (peel into each layer to reveal its own fact) so depth is experienced as a journey inward, not a flat list of three names.
keyRepresentations: Labelled cutaway sphere of Earth (crust, mantle, core) — the canonical diagram
Apple / hard-boiled-egg / peach analogy for the thin crust relative to the whole
A temperature gradient bar or colour ramp that heats up as you go deeper toward the core
A 'drill probe' descending inward, passing named layers, as a way to feel scale and depth
commonMisconceptions: The crust is thick / a large fraction of the Earth (it is a very thin skin by comparison).
The whole inside of the Earth is liquid lava/molten rock (much of the interior is solid or very stiff rock; the outer core is liquid metal, the inner core solid).
The centre is hollow, or filled with air/water, or that people/creatures could live inside.
'Lava' fills the Earth (magma forms only in specific hot regions; the term 'lava' applies only at the surface).
The layers are cold like ordinary underground soil (the interior is extremely hot, increasing with depth).

learn.summary: For ages 7–9, teach Earth's three named layers (crust, mantle, core) on a single labelled cutaway, then land the two real payloads: the crust is astonishingly THIN relative to the whole planet, and Earth's inside gets HOTTER with depth until it is hot enough to melt rock. Lead with a tap-to-reveal cutaway sphere that drills inward; support it with a driveable depth/temperature descent for a felt sense of thinness and heat, a nested 3D globe for scale extension, and a consolidation activity for naming and order. Guard against misconceptions that the crust is thick, that the whole interior is runny lava, or that the centre is hollow/cool — noting that much of the interior is solid rock and only the outer core is truly liquid.

activities.title: Drill-down cutaway: name the layers and feel the thin crust
feedback: If a child pictures the crust as thick as the mantle, show the to-scale slice: the crust is a hair-thin skin on a huge hot interior — like apple skin compared with the whole apple.
If a child thinks everything below the crust is runny liquid, clarify that the mantle is mostly solid, slow-flowing rock and that only the outer core is truly liquid metal, with the inner core solid.
If a child names the layers but is unsure of order, re-run the drill from the surface inward so crust→mantle→core is experienced as a journey, not a flat list.
Confirm success when the child names all three layers and states that the crust is the thinnest.
activities.rationale: The core evidence is naming three layers and attaching a fixed fact to each, which tap-to-reveal serves directly; building the thin-crust comparison as a zoom-out reveal makes the scale shock concrete and memorable. The apple-skin analogy gives a whole-object scale the child can hold in mind. The core fact card reflects a liquid outer core and solid inner core rather than a uniformly solid ball, consistent with the row's misconception notes.
sourceClaims: Earth's layers are crust (thin), mantle (thick, hot rock), and core (hottest, iron); temperature increases with depth.
learnerActions: Look at one labelled cutaway sphere of Earth showing crust, mantle and core named from the outside in.

Tap the crust to reveal its fact card (a thin rocky skin we stand on), tap the mantle to reveal 'thick, very hot, slow-flowing rock (mostly solid)', and tap the core to reveal 'the hottest part — a ball of iron whose outer part is liquid metal and whose very centre is solid'.
Lift a flap on the crust asking 'How thick is the crust really?' which zooms OUT and redraws the crust as a hair-thin line around the whole planet, captioned 'as thin as the skin on an apple'.
Say the three layers aloud from the outside in: crust, mantle, core.
activities.intendedInsight: Earth has three concentric layers, and the crust we live on is a very thin skin compared with the thick hot mantle and central core.

activities.title: Drill to the centre: hotter with depth
feedback: If a child thinks the interior is cool or only a bit warm, point to the climbing gauge and link to volcanoes and geothermal heat: the interior reaches thousands of degrees.
If a child over-estimates crust thickness, revisit the to-scale bar showing how briefly the drill was in the crust.
Reinforce that temperature rises continuously with depth, not just at the very centre.

If a child concludes that everything past the 'hot enough to melt rock' mark is molten, clarify that most of the deep rock stays solid under the enormous pressure — only the outer core is truly liquid — and that this heat is why magma can form in certain regions (keeping this consistent with the 'mantle is mostly solid' fact card).
activities.rationale: A driveable descent with live depth and temperature readouts makes 'hotter with depth' and 'thin crust' felt rather than told. The marker names the temperature threshold that is the stated payload, while the feedback keeps it coherent with the mostly-solid-mantle framing. This supports the tap-to-reveal model rather than replacing it; naming/reference remains the primary demand.
sourceClaims: Earth's layers are crust (thin), mantle (thick, hot rock), and core (hottest, iron); temperature increases with depth.
learnerActions: Drive a descending drill from the surface toward the centre, watching a live depth gauge and a temperature gauge.
Notice the crust is crossed almost immediately while the temperature keeps climbing — passing a marked point labelled 'hot enough to melt rock'.
Let each layer name itself (crust, mantle, core) as the drill passes it.
Afterwards, read a to-scale bar showing how little of the whole journey was the crust.
activities.intendedInsight: The deeper you go, the hotter it gets — hot enough to melt rock — and the crust occupies only a tiny fraction of the distance to the centre.

activities.title: Nested globe (scale extension)
feedback: If a child still draws the crust as a chunky layer, return to the to-scale shell and compare its thickness with the mantle.
Praise descriptions that capture the crust as a thin outer shell around a large hot interior.
activities.rationale: A rotatable, sliced 3D globe genuinely conveys concentric shells and relative scale. A flat cutaway already communicates the layer names, so treat the 3D view as a scale-focused extension that adds spatial polish here rather than a required insight for this particular payload.
learnerActions: Rotate a cut-open 3D globe to see the layers as concentric shells drawn to scale.
Pinch-zoom on the outer shell to feel how thin the crust is relative to the whole sphere.
Describe in your own words how much of the globe is crust versus everything beneath.
activities.intendedInsight: Earth is a nested sphere of concentric shells, and the crust shell is extremely thin compared with the interior.

activities.title: Consolidate names, order and facts
feedback: If the order is wrong, re-show the cutaway and name layers outward-to-inward.
If 'thinnest' is answered incorrectly, revisit the apple-skin scale reveal.
If the heat slider lands on 'warm' or 'boiling', state that the interior is hot enough to melt rock.
activities.rationale: Sequencing, labelling and targeted multiple-choice consolidate names, order and the thin/hot facts. This mainly checks and reinforces recall rather than building the initial insight, so use it after the model-based activities.
learnerActions: Sequence the layers from outside in: crust → mantle → core.
Answer 'Which layer is thinnest?' and 'Which is hottest?'
Use a slider to answer 'How hot is it deep down — warm, boiling, or hot enough to melt rock?'
Label a blank cutaway diagram with crust, mantle and core.
activities.intendedInsight: The learner can reliably recall the three layer names, their order, which is thinnest, and that the interior is hot enough to melt rock.

constraints: In England there is no KS2 science requirement on Earth's internal structure; 'composition of the Earth' and 'structure of the Earth' are KS3 Chemistry. At KS2 this content sits in Geography (volcanoes and earthquakes) and builds on Y3 Rocks. Treat as an enrichment/Geography-linked topic that runs ahead of the KS2 science sequence.

In NGSS, Earth's interior structure and plate tectonics are treated at middle school (MS-ESS2), not as a standalone elementary performance expectation; nearest young-learner touchpoints are 2-ESS1-1 and 4-ESS2-2.
Prerequisite is 'Earth Is Made of Rock' (ages 5–7).
Keep the model singular and stable: introduce all three layers on ONE cutaway before adding facts.
The consolidation activity checks recall of names, order and facts; it does not by itself build the thin-crust scale insight, which needs the model-based reveal.
The 3D globe is an optional scale extension; the flat cutaway is sufficient to communicate the layer names for this payload.

Do not imply the whole interior is liquid lava: the mantle is mostly solid, soft, slow-flowing rock; only the outer core is truly liquid metal and the inner core is solid. Do not describe the core as a uniformly solid ball either.
Present 'hot enough to melt rock' as a temperature fact; make clear that much of the deep rock nonetheless stays solid under pressure, so the marker is not evidence of a molten interior.
Reserve the word 'lava' for molten rock at the surface; magma forms only in specific hot regions underground.
Depth gauges, temperature gauges, lift-the-flap reveals, pinch-zoom and sliders are example interaction mechanisms to make scale and heat concrete; they are illustrative, not mandatory.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three source claims are marked unverified in the row (the NGSS MS-ESS2 placement claim and the USGS/National Geographic layer-structure claim); only the DfE KS3-placement claim is marked verified. Treat the layer facts and NGSS placement as unconfirmed here.

The original recommendation described the core as a 'solid iron ball'; this was corrected in learner-facing text to reflect a liquid outer core and a solid inner core, consistent with the row's own misconception list. The source claim only states 'hottest, iron' and does not establish a uniformly solid core.

The original entry asserted '3D adds spatial polish rather than a required insight' and that the quiz 'assesses rather than teaches'; these have been softened to scoped roles (extension and consolidation for this payload) rather than universal laws about those media.

Characterising the mantle as 'solid' is a simplification for ages 7–9; it is better described as stiff, slow-flowing (plastic) rock. The activities use child-friendly language ('mostly solid, slow-flowing') and avoid asserting the whole interior is liquid.

The 'hot enough to melt rock' depth marker was kept from the original but framed as a temperature threshold, with added feedback that pressure keeps most deep rock solid, to avoid contradicting the mostly-solid-mantle fact card.
Age-appropriate temperature claims (interior 'thousands of degrees', 'hot enough to melt rock') follow the source but were not independently verified in this rewrite.

probeDeeper: If the whole Earth were the size of an apple, how thick would the crust be?
Why is it hot enough deep down to melt rock into magma?
Name the three main layers from the outside in.
Is everything below the crust runny liquid, or is some of it solid?
assess.correctAnswer: We stand on the crust, the outermost layer. It's extremely THIN compared with the layers below — like the skin on an apple compared with the whole apple. Beneath it is the thick, very hot mantle, and at the centre the core. The inside of the Earth is hot enough to melt rock.

errorPatterns.pattern: The crust is thick — a big chunky layer about the same as the others
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show a to-scale slice — the crust is a hair-thin skin on a huge hot interior.
errorPatterns.distractor: The crust is a thick layer, about the same as the others.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws or describes the crust roughly as thick as the mantle.

errorPatterns.pattern: The inside of the Earth is cool, or only a bit warm
errorPatterns.nextMove: Link to volcanoes and geothermal heat — the interior is thousands of degrees.
errorPatterns.distractor: The inside of the Earth is cool or only a bit warm.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies the interior is hot enough to melt rock.

errorPatterns.pattern: The whole inside of the Earth is runny liquid / molten
errorPatterns.nextMove: The mantle is mostly solid hot rock (soft, slow-flowing); only the outer core is truly liquid.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says everything under the crust is liquid.

responseLevels.gap: Can't name the layers, or thinks the crust is thick and the interior cool.
responseLevels.full: Names the layers, explains the crust is very thin (apple-skin) compared with the thick hot mantle and central core, and states the interior is hot enough to melt rock.
responseLevels.partial: Names crust/mantle/core and says the interior is hot, but pictures the crust as thick or is unsure of the scale.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Imagine a slice cut through the whole Earth, from the surface down to the centre. Which layer are we standing on, and how thick is it compared with the layers underneath?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child can name crust/mantle/core (first tier) yet picture the crust as a thick slab. Asking about relative thickness forces the apple-skin insight; a child who over-thickens the crust reveals the common scale misconception.
